assumptions: let $(\pi,X)$ be an irreducible $\mathbb{H}$-module

nodes.name: Casimir element of S~_n
nodes.statement: \cite[3.4]{BCT12}The Casimir element for $\tilde{S_n}$ is $$\Omega_{\tilde{S_n}} = \frac{1}{4}\sum_{\begin{substack}{\alpha, \beta \in \Phi^+\\ s_\alpha(\beta) < 0} \end{substack}} |\alpha||\beta| \tau_\alpha \tau_\beta,$$ where $\tau_\alpha$ is the generator of $\tilde{S_n}$ corresponding to $\alpha$. In \cite{BCT12} $\Omega_{\tilde{S}}$ is negative but we define it as positive since we have the positive form on $C(V)$.

nodes.name: Casimir of S~_n is central
nodes.statement: The Casimir $\Omega_{\tilde{S}_n}$ is central in $\mathbb{C}[\tilde{S}_n]$, \cite{BCT12}.

nodes.name: Square of the Dirac element
nodes.statement: \cite[3.5]{BCT12} As elements of $\mathbb{H}\otimes C(V)$, $$\mathcal{D}^2 = \Omega_\mathbb{H}\otimes 1- \rho(\Omega_{\tilde{S_n}}),$$
nodes.statement_short: D^2 = Omega_H tensor 1 - rho(Omega_{S~_n}) in H tensor C(V).
nodes.label: Dirac

nodes.name: Steinberg module
nodes.statement: \cite{Ci16} We introduce the one dimensional $\mathbb{H}$-module, called the Steinberg module $St$. Here $S_n$ acts on $St$ by the $\mathrm{sgn}$ character and $\xi_i\in S(V)$ act by $\frac{n-1 + 2i}{2}$.
nodes.label: Steinberg

nodes.name: Standard module X_lambda
nodes.statement: Let $X_\lambda$ be the parabolically induced $\mathbb{H}$-module from the Steinberg module for $\mathbb{H}_{\lambda_1}\times \ldots \times \mathbb{H}_{\lambda_k}$, $$X_\lambda = \mathrm{Ind}_{\mathbb{H}_{\lambda_1}\times \ldots \times \mathbb{H}_{\lambda_k}}^\mathbb{H} (St_{\lambda_1} \otimes \ldots \otimes St_{\lambda_k}).$$

nodes.name: V_lambda inside the Dirac cohomology of X_lambda
nodes.statement: In \cite[5.8]{BCT12} it is shown that, inside the Dirac cohomology of $X_\lambda$, one can find the genuine projective irreducible representation $V_\lambda$ of isomorphism class associated to a shifted partition $\lambda \vDash n$.

nodes.name: D^2 acts by zero on Dirac cohomology
nodes.statement: Since $H_D(X)$ is a quotient of $\ker(D)$, $D^2$ acts by zero on $H_D(X)$.

nodes.name: Casimir elements agree on Dirac cohomology
nodes.statement: On the Dirac cohomology (resp. extended Dirac index), or any submodule found inside it, namely $V_\lambda$ (resp. $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$), $$\Omega_\mathbb{H}\otimes 1= \rho(\Omega_{\tilde{W}}).$$

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 3.16
nodes.statement: This follows from $D^2$ acting by zero and the equation given in Theorem \ref{Dirac}.
nodes.statement_short: D^2 acts by zero; apply the formula for D^2 of Theorem 3.13.

nodes.name: Green polynomial character p^lambda(q)
nodes.statement: \cite[I.7]{GP92} Let $p^\lambda (q)$ be the character of the graded $S_n$-module $$\sum_{i\geq0} \textbf{q}^i H^{2i}(\mathcal{B}_\lambda ).$$

nodes.name: Garsia-Procesi reduction rule
nodes.statement: \cite[1.1]{GP92} Let $\lambda = (\lambda_1,\ldots ,\lambda_r)$ be a fixed partition of $n$ and $\lambda' = (\lambda_1',\ldots ,\lambda_r')$ be its conjugate. For $1 \leq i \leq l(\lambda)$ define the integer $a_i$ by the condition $$\lambda_{a_i}' \geq i > \lambda_{a_i+1}'.$$ Given this integer, let $\lambda^{(i)}$ be the partition created when one removes a block from the bottom of column $a_i$ of the Young diagram associated to $\lambda$.
nodes.statement_short: lambda^(i) removes a box from the bottom of column a_i, where lambda'_{a_i} >= i > lambda'_{a_i+1}.

nodes.name: Set Theta of partitions obtained by removing a box
nodes.statement: Given $\lambda \vdash n$, let $\Theta^n_{n-1}(\lambda)$ be the set of partitions of $n-1$ which one can create from the Young diagram of $\lambda$ by removing a single box.

nodes.name: Reduction rule for strict partitions
nodes.statement: For a strict partition $\lambda = (\lambda_1,\ldots ,\lambda_r) \vdash n$ we have $$\lambda^{(i)} = (\lambda_1,\ldots ,\lambda_{i-1},\lambda_{i} -1 , \lambda_{i+1},\ldots ,\lambda_r).$$ Hence $\{\lambda^{(i)} : i =1,\ldots ,l(\lambda) \}$ is equal to the set $\Theta^n_{n-1}(\lambda)$.
assumptions: For a strict partition $\lambda = (\lambda_1,\ldots ,\lambda_r) \vdash n$
conclusions: Hence $\{\lambda^{(i)} : i =1,\ldots ,l(\lambda) \}$ is equal to the set $\Theta^n_{n-1}(\lambda)$.
nodes.statement_short: For strict lambda, lambda^(i) removes a box from row i, so the lambda^(i) are exactly the one-box removals.
nodes.label: strictset

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.3
nodes.statement: Because $\lambda$ is strict, the column of $\lambda$ which is first larger than $i$, $\lambda_{a_i}'$, will always be the column that has a block from $\lambda_1,\ldots ,\lambda_i$ and no others. So removing a block from row $\lambda_i$ is equivalent to removing a block from column $\lambda_{a_i}'$. Hence $\lambda^{(i)} = (\lambda_1,\ldots ,\lambda_{i-1},\lambda_{i} -1 , \lambda_{i+1},\ldots ,\lambda_r)$. The second statement follows since we have an explicit description of $\{\lambda^{(i)} : i =1,\ldots ,l(\lambda) \}$.
nodes.statement_short: For strict lambda the column a_i contains only blocks of rows 1..i, so removing from column a_i equals removing from row i.

nodes.name: Restriction functor Res^n_{n-1}
nodes.statement: Given a module or character $A$ of either $S_n$, $\tilde{S}_n$ or $C(n)$, let $\mathrm{Res}_{n-1}^n(A)$ denote the restriction to the rank $({n-1})$ object, that is the restriction to $S_{n-1}$, $\tilde{S}_{n-1}$ or $C(n-1)$.

nodes.name: Garsia-Procesi branching rule
nodes.statement: \cite[3.3]{GP92} The restriction of the $S_n$ $\textbf{q}$-graded character $p^\lambda(\textbf{q})$ to $S_{n-1}$ is a sum of $\textbf{q}^{i-1}p^{\lambda^{(i)}}(\textbf{q})$; $$\mathrm{Res}^n_{n-1}p^\lambda(\textbf{q}) = \sum_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)} \textbf{q}^{i-1} p^{\lambda^{(i)}}(\textbf{q}).$$
nodes.statement_short: Restricting p^lambda(q) to S_{n-1} gives the sum of q^{i-1} p^{lambda^(i)}(q).
nodes.label: GPbranching

nodes.name: Character of X_q(lambda) via reversed grading
nodes.statement: If we let $\chi_{\textbf{q}} (\lambda)$ be the character of $X_{\textbf{q}}(\lambda)$ then $$\chi_{\textbf{q}} (\lambda ) = p^\lambda (\boldsymbol{\frac{1}{q}}) q^{n(\lambda)} $$ where $n(\lambda) = \sum_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)} (i-1)\lambda_i$.
assumptions: If we let $\chi_{\textbf{q}} (\lambda)$ be the character of $X_{\textbf{q}}(\lambda)$
nodes.statement_short: chi_q(lambda) = p^lambda(1/q) q^{n(lambda)} with n(lambda) = sum (i-1) lambda_i.
nodes.label: reverse

nodes.name: Branching of X_q(lambda)
nodes.statement: Let $\lambda$ be a strict partition. The restriction of the $S_n$-module $X_{\textbf{q}}(\lambda)$ to $S_{n-1}$ is $$Res^{n}_{n-1} X_{\textbf{q}}(\lambda) = \bigoplus_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)} \textbf{q}^{2i-2}X_{\textbf{q}}(\lambda^{(i)}).$$
assumptions: Let $\lambda$ be a strict partition.
nodes.statement_short: For strict lambda, Res X_q(lambda) = sum of q^{2i-2} X_q(lambda^(i)).
nodes.label: qres

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.6
nodes.statement: By Remark \ref{reverse} one can write $\chi_\textbf{q}(\lambda) = p^\lambda (\boldsymbol{\frac{1}{q}}) q^{n(\lambda)}$. Then, we can use the restriction rules given by Theorem \ref{GPbranching} to restrict $\chi_\textbf{q}(\lambda)$ in terms of the characters $p^{\lambda^{(i)}}(\textbf{q})$. Remark \ref{reverse} can be used again to rewrite this in terms of characters $\chi_{\textbf{q}}(\lambda^{(i)})$. The coefficient one gets is $\textbf{q}^{i-1+ n(\lambda) - n(\lambda^{(i)})}$. Writing out the definition of $n(\lambda)$; $$n(\lambda) - n(\lambda^{(i)}) = \sum_{j=1}^l(\lambda)(j-1)\lambda_j - \sum_{j=1}^{l(\lambda^{(i)})} (j-1)\lambda^{(i)}_j.$$ However, by Lemma \ref{strictset}, $\lambda$ and $\lambda^{(i)}$ differ by only one entry for $\lambda$ strict. This difference is in the $ith$ entry. Therefore $n(\lambda)$ and $n(\lambda^{(i)})$ differ by $i-1$. Hence $i-1+ n(\lambda) - n(\lambda^{(i)}) = 2i-2$.
nodes.statement_short: Reverse the grading via Remark 4.5, apply Garsia-Procesi branching, and compute the q-exponent using Lemma 4.3.

nodes.name: Branching of X_{-1}(lambda)
nodes.statement: Let $\lambda$ be a strict partition. The restriction of the graded $S_n$-module $X_{-1}(\lambda)$ is, $$Res^{n}_{n-1} X_{-1}(\lambda) = \bigoplus_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)} X_{-1}(\lambda^{(i)}).$$
assumptions: Let $\lambda$ be a strict partition.
nodes.statement_short: Specialising q=-1: Res X_{-1}(lambda) is the direct sum of the X_{-1}(lambda^(i)).
nodes.label: summands

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.7
nodes.statement: This is the specialisation of Lemma \ref{qres} to $\textbf{q} = -1$.
nodes.statement_short: Specialise Lemma 4.6 to q = -1.

nodes.name: Transversal of irreducible genuine projective supermodules
nodes.statement: The set $\{\tilde{\tau}_\lambda : \lambda \text{ is strict}\}$ is a transversal for the irreducible genuine projective supermodules of $S_n$.
conclusions: The set $\{\tilde{\tau}_\lambda : \lambda \text{ is strict}\}$ is a transversal for the irreducible genuine projective supermodules of $S_n$.

nodes.name: Strict lambda^(i) occur in the restriction of tau~_lambda
nodes.statement: Let $\lambda$ be a strict partition. For a fixed $i$, if $\lambda^{(i)}$ is strict then $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda^{(i)}$ is a summand of $\mathrm{Res}_{n-1}^n(\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$).
assumptions: Let $\lambda$ be a strict partition.
if $\lambda^{(i)}$ is strict

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.8
nodes.statement: We note that $a_\lambda \tilde{\tau}_\lambda = X_{-1}(\lambda) \otimes \mathcal{S}$. Here, $\mathcal{S}$ (resp. $\mathcal{S}'$) is the spinor supermodule for the Clifford algebra $C(n)$ (resp. $C(n-1)$). Hence restricting $a_\lambda \tilde{\tau_\lambda} $ to $\tilde{S}_{n-1}$ is equivalent to restricting $X_{-1}(\lambda)$ to $S_{n-1}$ and $\mathcal{S}$ to $C(n-1)$. Therefore $$a_\lambda Res^{n}_{n-1} \tilde{\tau}_\lambda = Res^{n}_{n-1}\mathcal{S} \otimes Res^{n}_{n-1} X_{-1}(\lambda) $$ $$= c \mathcal{S}' \otimes \bigoplus_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)} X_{-1}(\lambda^{(i)}).$$ $$= \bigoplus_{{\lambda^{(i)}} \text{ which are strict }} c\mathcal{S}' \otimes X_{-1}(\lambda^{(i)}).$$ Here, $c \in \mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}$ and will be determined in Theorem \ref{branchingrules}. Hence, for every strict $\lambda^{(i)}$ the $\tilde{S}_n$ supermodule $\tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(i)}}$ occurs as a summand.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict X_{-1}(lambda) and the spinor separately; non-strict summands are killed by the spinor.

nodes.name: Branching rules for genuine projective supermodules of S~_n
nodes.statement: The branching rules of the genuine projective irreducible $\tilde{S}_n$-supermodules are $$Res^{n}_{n-1} \tilde{\tau}_\lambda = \begin{cases} 2\tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(1)}}\oplus 2\tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(2)}}\oplus \ldots \oplus 2\tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(r-1)}}\oplus \tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(r)}} & \text{ if } n-r \text{ is odd and } \lambda_r = 1, \\ 2\tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(1)}}\oplus 2\tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(2)}}\oplus \ldots \oplus 2\tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(r-1)}}\oplus 2\tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(r)}} & \text{ if } n-r \text{ is odd and } \lambda_r > 1, \\ \tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(1)}}\oplus \tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(2)}}\oplus \ldots \oplus \tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(r-1)}}\oplus \tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(r)}} & \text{ if } n-r \text{ is even.}\end{cases}$$ Here $\lambda$ is always a strict partition.
also_stated_at: The branching rules of the genuine projective irreducible $\tilde{S}_n$-supermodules are: $$Res^{n}_{n-1} \tilde{\tau}_\lambda = \begin{cases} 2\tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(1)}}\oplus 2\tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(2)}}\oplus \ldots \oplus 2\tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(r-1)}}\oplus \tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(r)}} & \text{ if } n-r \text{ is odd and } \lambda_r = 1, \\ 2\tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(1)}}\oplus 2\tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(2)}}\oplus \ldots \oplus 2\tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(r-1)}}\oplus 2\tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(r)}} & \text{ if } n-r \text{ is odd and } \lambda_r > 1, \\ \tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(1)}}\oplus \tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(2)}}\oplus \ldots \oplus \tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(r-1)}}\oplus \tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(r)}} & \text{ if } n-r \text{ is even.}\end{cases}$$ Here $\lambda$ is always a strict partition.
assumptions: Here $\lambda$ is always a strict partition.
nodes.statement_short: Res tau~_lambda is the sum of tau~_{lambda^(i)} with multiplicities 1 or 2 depending on the parity of n-r and whether lambda_r = 1.
nodes.label: branchingrules

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.9
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{summands} we already know which summands will occur. Hence calculating the multiplicities is all that is required. We know the multiplicities of the restriction of the spinor $S_n$; $2$ if $n$ is even, $1$ otherwise. Also, by Lemma \ref{summands} the multiplicities in the restriction of $X_{-1}(\lambda)$ are always $1$. Hence, we can find the multiplicities for $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ by comparing $\frac{1}{a_\lambda}$ and $\frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}}$ from Proposition \ref{alambda}. This is a simple calculation on the eight cases $$\frac{1}{a_\lambda} = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2} \frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ even, } l(\lambda) \text{ even and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda),\\ \frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ even, } l(\lambda) \text{ even and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda)-1,\\ \frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ even, } l(\lambda) \text{ odd and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda),\\ \frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ even, } l(\lambda) \text{ odd and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda)-1,\\ 2\frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}}& n \text{ odd, } l(\lambda) \text{ even and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda),\\ \frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ odd, } l(\lambda) \text{ even and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda)-1,\\ \frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ odd, } l(\lambda) \text{ odd and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda),\\ \frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ odd, } l(\lambda) \text{ odd and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda)-1.\\ \end{cases}$$ Note that $l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda)-1$ occurs once if and only if $\lambda_r = 1$, in which case it is the partition $\lambda^{(r)}$ which has shorter length.
nodes.statement_short: Summands are known from Lemma 4.7; multiplicities follow by comparing the normalising constants a_lambda over eight parity cases.

nodes.name: Jucys-Murphy elements in T_n
nodes.statement: \cite[3.1]{BK01} The Jucys-Murphy elements in $\mathcal{T}_n$ for $i=1,\ldots ,n$ are, $$M_i = \sum_{\alpha \in \Phi^+ : ( \alpha , \xi_i ) < 0} \tau_\alpha.$$ This is the same construction as the Jucys-Murphy elements for $S_n$. We have just replaced transpositions with pseudo-transpositions.

nodes.name: Jucys-Murphy elements anti-commute
nodes.statement: The Jucys-Murphys elements anti-commute \cite[3.1]{BK01}, that is $$M_kM_l = -M_lM_k \text{ if } k \neq l.$$
nodes.label: anti-commute

nodes.name: Even centre of T_n
nodes.statement: \cite[3.2]{BK01} The even centre $Z(\mathcal{T}_n)_0$ of $\mathcal{T}_n$ is spanned by the set of symmetric polynomials of the Jucys-Murphy elements.

nodes.name: Schur's classification of projective characters
nodes.statement: Schur (cf. \cite{S89}) defined all of the genuine projective characters for $\tilde{S}_n$, and he showed that these correspond to the set of shifted partitions $\lambda \in \mathcal{SP}(n)$.

nodes.name: Module V_lambda
nodes.statement: Let $V_\lambda$ denote any genuine projective $\tilde{S}_n$-module which has character corresponding to $\lambda \in \mathcal{SP}(n)$.

nodes.name: Function q(m) = m(m+1)
nodes.statement: It will be useful, for notation, to introduce a function $q:\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ such that $q(m) = m(m+1)$.

nodes.name: Spectrum set Sspec(n)
nodes.statement: \cite{VS08} We say $\alpha = (\alpha_1,\ldots ,\alpha_n)$ is in $\mathrm{Sspec}(n)$ if there exists a vector $v$ in an irreducible genuine projective representation $V$ of $\tilde{S}_n$ such that: $$M_k^2 v = \frac{1}{2}q(a_k) v \text{ for all } k=1,\ldots ,n.$$ $\mathrm{Sspec}(n, \lambda)$ is the restriction of $\mathrm{Sspec}(n)$ by considering vectors in any $V_\lambda$, $\lambda \in \mathcal{SP}(n)$.
nodes.statement_short: Sspec(n): vectors alpha with a vector v in a genuine projective irrep on which M_k^2 acts by q(alpha_k)/2 for all k.
nodes.label: spec

nodes.name: Content of a box in a shifted diagram
nodes.statement: Let $\lambda \in \mathcal{SP}(n)$ be a shifted partition.The content of a box $(i,j)$ contained in a shifted Young diagram $\lambda$ is its distance from the main diagonal. $$\mathrm{cont}(i,j) = j-i$$

nodes.name: Shifted content vectors Scont(n)
nodes.statement: We introduce the set of shifted content vectors $\mathrm{Scont}(n)$. A vector $\beta = (\beta_1,\ldots ,\beta_n)$ is associated to a standard shifted tableaux $[[\lambda]]$ if, for all $i=1,\ldots ,n$, $\beta_i$ is equal to the content of the box labelled i in $[[\lambda]]$. $\mathrm{Scont}(n)$ is the set of vectors which are associated to a standard shifted tableau of size n. Similarly $\mathrm{Scont}(n,\lambda)$, is the set of vectors associated to standard shifted tableaux of shape $\lambda$.
nodes.statement_short: Scont(n): content vectors of standard shifted tableaux of size n (Scont(n, lambda) for shape lambda).

nodes.name: Central character
nodes.statement: A central character is a map $Z(\mathbb{H}) = S(V)^W \to \mathbb{C}$.

nodes.name: Central character chi_lambda of X_lambda
nodes.statement: The standard representations $X_\lambda$ have central characters $\chi_\lambda$.

nodes.name: Central character of the Steinberg module
nodes.statement:
Let $St_m$ be the Steinberg module for $\mathbb{H}_m$. Let $
u_{St_m}$ be the element in $S(V)^*/W$ corresponding to $\chi_{St_m}$ . Let $e_1,\ldots ,e_m \in V^*$ be a a dual basis of the basis $x_1,..,x_m$ of $V$. The element $
u_{\mathrm{St}_m}$ is, $$
u_{\mathrm{St}_m} = - rac{m-1}{2}e_1 + - rac{m-3}{2}e_2+\ldots + rac{m-3}{2}e_{m-1} +  rac{m-1}{2}e_m = \sum_{i=1}^m  rac{2i-m}{2}e_i.$$
nodes.statement_short: The Steinberg module St_m has central character nu = sum (2i-m)/2 e_i.

nodes.name: Central character of X_lambda
nodes.statement:
The element $
u_\lambda$ defining the central character of $X_\lambda$ is $$
u = \sum_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)} 
u_{\mathrm{St}_{\lambda_i}}.$$

nodes.name: Casimir of H on X_lambda
nodes.statement: \cite[2.5]{BCT12} On the representation $X_\lambda$ of the graded Hecke algebra $\mathbb{H}$, $$\Omega_\mathbb{H} = ( \nu , \nu ).$$
assumptions: On the representation $X_\lambda$ of the graded Hecke algebra $\mathbb{H}$
nodes.label: HOmega

nodes.name: Casimir of H on tau~_lambda via contents
nodes.statement: On the representation $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ corresponding to $\lambda = (\lambda_1,\ldots ,\lambda_r)$, $$\Omega_\mathbb{H} = \sum_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)} \sum_{j=1}^{\lambda_i} (\frac{2j - \lambda_i}{2})^2.$$ Furthermore, this can be reformulated in terms of the content of $\lambda$, $$ \Omega_\mathbb{H} =\frac{1}{4} \sum_{(i,j) \in \lambda} q(\mathrm{cont}(i,j)).$$
nodes.statement_short: On tau~_lambda, Omega_H acts by a sum over boxes, equal to 1/4 sum of q(cont(i,j)) over the shifted diagram.
nodes.label: content

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.11
nodes.statement: The first part can be proved by noticing that, when one forgets the grading, the module $X_{-1}(\lambda)$ is just the parabolically induced module $X_\lambda$, see \cite{BM83}. Hence, one can use Lemma \ref{HOmega} to show how $\Omega_\mathbb{H}$ acts. The constant $( \nu, \nu )$ is exactly the sum we stated. The second part follows by a simple induction. One can show $\sum_{j=1}^{\lambda_i} (2j - \lambda_i)^2= \sum_{j=1}^{\lambda_i} j(j+1) = \sum_{j=1}^{\lambda_k} q(\mathrm{cont}(k,j))$, splitting the cases when $\lambda_i$ is odd or even. This will be covered in more detail in Section \ref{vogan}.
nodes.statement_short: Identify X_{-1}(lambda) with X_lambda and apply Lemma 5.10; the content form follows by a simple induction.

nodes.name: Casimir of S~_n as sum of squares of Jucys-Murphy elements
nodes.statement: In the algebra $\mathcal{T}_n$, the Casimir element, $\Omega_{\tilde{S}_n} =\frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^n M_k^2$. Here $M_k$ denotes the Jucys-Murphy elements for $\mathcal{T}_n$.
also_stated_at: On genuine projective representations $\Omega_{\tilde{S}_n} =\frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^n M_k^2$. Here $M_k$ denotes the Jucys-Murphy elements for $\tilde{S}_n$.
assumptions: In the algebra $\mathcal{T}_n$
nodes.label: squares

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.12
nodes.statement: $$\Omega_{\tilde{S}_n}= \frac{1}{4}\sum_{\substack{\alpha,\beta\in\Phi^+ \\ s_\alpha(\beta)<0}} |\alpha||\beta|\tau_\alpha \tau_\beta $$ $$=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{\alpha,\beta\in \Phi^+} |\alpha||\beta|\tau_\alpha \tau_\beta= \frac{1}{4}(\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}|\alpha|\tau_\alpha)^2$$ $$=\frac{1}{4} (\sum_{k=1}^{n}|\alpha|M_k)^2= \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^n M_k^2$$ In the second equality, we use $\tau_\alpha \tau_\beta = - \tau_\beta \tau_{s_\alpha(\beta)}$ for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ such that $s_\alpha(\beta)>0$. The third equality uses the fact that every $\sum_{i=1}^n M_k = \sum_{\alpha \in \Phi^+} \tau_\alpha$ and the last equality uses the fact that the Jucys-Murphy elements anti-commute in $\mathcal{T}_n$ \cite[3.1]{BK01}. Hence the square of the sum is equal to the sum of the squares.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the Casimir as the square of the sum of pseudo-transpositions, i.e. of the Jucys-Murphy elements, and use anti-commutation.

nodes.name: Spectrum data equals shifted content data
nodes.statement: The set $\mathrm{Sspec}(n) \subset \mathbb{N}^n$ is equal to the set $\mathrm{Scont}(n)$. Further, $$\mathrm{Sspec}(n,\lambda) = \mathrm{Scont}(n,\lambda).$$
also_stated_at: The set $\mathrm{Sspec}(n) \subset \mathbb{N}^n$, descending from eigenvalues of Jucys-Murphy elements, is equal to the set $\mathrm{Scont}(n)$, a combinatorial construction from contents of shifted Young tableaux. Further, $$\mathrm{Sspec}(n,\lambda) \cong \mathrm{Scont}(n,\lambda).$$
conclusions: The set $\mathrm{Sspec}(n) \subset \mathbb{N}^n$ is equal to the set $\mathrm{Scont}(n)$.
nodes.statement_short: The Jucys-Murphy spectrum of genuine projective representations equals the set of content vectors of standard shifted tableaux.
nodes.label: spectrumdata

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.13
nodes.statement: We prove the theorem by induction, the base case being trivial. Suppose for every shifted partition $\mu \in \mathcal{SP}(n-1)$, $\mathrm{Scont}(n-1, \mu) = \mathrm{Sspec}(n-1, \mu)$. Let us fix a shifted partition $\lambda$ of $n$, and consider $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ the irreducible representation of $\mathcal{T}_n$ associated to $\lambda$. Let $\alpha = (\alpha_1,\ldots ,\alpha_n)\in \mathrm{Sspec}(n , \lambda)$. By definition there exists a vector $v_\alpha \in \tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ such that $M_j^2(v_\alpha) =q(\alpha_j )v_\alpha \text{ for all } $j$.$ The restriction of $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ to $\mathcal{T}_{n-1}$ is the direct sum, $\bigoplus_{i =1}^{l(\lambda)} \tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(i)}}$. Also $v_\alpha$ is an eigenvector for the Jucys-Murphys elements. Hence $v_\alpha \in \tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(j)}} \subset \tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ for some fixed $j$. We know, by the inductive hypothesis, $(\alpha_1,\ldots ,\alpha_{n-1}) \in \mathrm{Sspec}(n-1,\lambda^{(j)}) = \mathrm{Scont}(n-1,\lambda^{(j)})$. Explicitly, this means there exists a standard numbering $[[\lambda^{(j)}]]$ of $\lambda^{(j)}$ which corresponds to $(\alpha_1,\ldots ,\alpha_{n-1})$. Now using Lemma \ref{content}, Lemma \ref{squares} and Theorem \ref{Dirac}, we can describe the action of the Casimir elements of $\tilde{S}_n$ and $\tilde{S}_{n-1}$ on $v_\alpha$. Since $v_\alpha$ is in $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ , $$ \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^n M_k^2 v_\alpha = \Omega_{\tilde{S}_n} v_\alpha= \Omega_{\mathbb{H}_n}v_\alpha =\frac{1}{4} \sum_{(i,j) \in \lambda} \mathrm{cont}(i,j)(\mathrm{cont}(i,j)+1)v_\alpha. $$ However $v_\alpha$ is also contained in $\tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(j)}}\subset \tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ so, $$\frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} M_k^2v_\alpha = \Omega_{\tilde{S}_{n-1}} v_\alpha= \Omega_{\mathbb{H}_{n-1}}v_\alpha =\frac{1}{4} \sum_{(i,j) \in \lambda^{(j)}} \mathrm{cont}(i,j)(\mathrm{cont}(i,j)+1)v_\alpha.$$ the difference of these two Casimir elements is $\frac{1}{2}M_n^2$. Hence $$M_n^2 v_\alpha = \left(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{(i,j) \in \lambda} \mathrm{cont}(i,j)(\mathrm{cont}(i,j)+1) - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{(i,j) \in \lambda^{(j)}} \mathrm{cont}(i,j)(\mathrm{cont}(i,j)+1) \right) v_\alpha$$ $$ =\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{cont}(k,l)(\mathrm{cont}(k,l)+ 1)v_\alpha,$$ where $(k,l)$ is the block of $ \lambda $ not included in $ \lambda^{(i)}.$ Taking the standard shifted tableau $[[\lambda^{(j)}]]_{(\alpha_1,\ldots ,\alpha_{n-1})}$ associated to $(\alpha_1,\ldots ,\alpha_{n-1})$ and adding the block $(k,l)$ labelled with the number $n$ creates a standard shifted tableau $[[\lambda]]_\alpha$ of shape $\lambda$. By the above argument this standard shifted tableau has content vector equal to $\alpha \in \mathrm{Sspec}(n,\lambda)$. Hence $\alpha \in \mathrm{Scont}(n,\lambda)$. For the reverse direction, we use an almost identical argument. Suppose $\beta =(\beta_1,\ldots ,\beta_n) \in \mathrm{Scont}(n,\lambda)$ corresponds to a standard shifted tableau $[[\lambda]]_\beta$. By restriction and inductive hypothesis, there exists a vector $v_{(\beta_1,\ldots ,\beta_{n-1})} \in \tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(j)}} \subset \tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ such that $M_k^2 v_{(\beta_1,\ldots ,\beta_{n-1})} = q(\beta_k) v_{(\beta_1,\ldots ,\beta_{n-1})}$. Again using the fact that $M_n^2$ acts by the difference of the Casimir elements $\Omega_{S_n}$ and $\Omega_{S_{n-1}}$, we get, $$M_n^2 v_{(\beta_1,\ldots ,\beta_{n-1})} = 2(\Omega_{\tilde{S}_n} - \Omega_{\tilde{S}_{n-1}}) = \frac{1}{2}q(\mathrm{cont}(n))v_{(\beta_1,\ldots ,\beta_{n-1})},$$ where $\mathrm{cont}(n)$ is the content of the box labelled by $n$ in $[[\lambda]]_\beta$. Hence $\beta \in Spec(n,\lambda)$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on n via the branching rule. M_n^2 acts by the difference of the Casimirs of S~_n and S~_{n-1}, computed through Dirac cohomology as the content of the added box.

nodes.name: Jucys-Murphy subalgebra
nodes.statement: Let $\langle M_1,\ldots ,M_n \rangle$ be the subalgebra of $\mathbb{C}[\tilde{S}_n]$ generated by the Jucys-Murphy elements $M_i$.

nodes.name: Restriction to the Jucys-Murphy subalgebra splits into eigenspaces
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a genuine irreducible projective representation of $\tilde{S}_n$. Then the restriction of $V$ to $\langle M_1,\ldots ,M_n \rangle$ is a direct sum of the common eigenspaces of $M_i^2$.
assumptions: Let $V$ be a genuine irreducible projective representation of $\tilde{S}_n$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.1
nodes.statement: The $M_i^2$ all commute so we can separate $V$ into its common eigenspaces. Now $M_i$ fix these spaces so the common eigenspaces are $\langle M_1,\ldots ,M_n \rangle$ submodules of $V$.
nodes.statement_short: The M_i^2 commute, so V splits into common eigenspaces, which the M_i preserve.

nodes.name: Eigenspaces are Clifford modules
nodes.statement: Let $U$ be an $\langle M_1,\ldots ,M_n \rangle$-supermodule which occurs as a common eigenspace of $M_i^2$ in some $V$. Then the the representation $U$ of $\langle M_1,\ldots ,M_n \rangle$ factors through the Clifford algebra of rank $r$, where $r = |\{M_i^2 \text{ with non zero eigenvalue}\}| = n - l(\lambda)$.
assumptions: Let $U$ be an $\langle M_1,\ldots ,M_n \rangle$-supermodule which occurs as a common eigenspace of $M_i^2$ in some $V$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.2
nodes.statement: The set of Jucys-Murphy elements anti-commute and on $U$, by Definition \ref{spec}, $M_i^2 = q(\alpha_i)$ for some $\alpha = (\alpha_1,\ldots ,\alpha_n) \in \mathrm{Sspec}(n)$. By sending $M_i$ to $\frac{c_i}{\sqrt{q(\alpha_i)}}$ for $\alpha_i \neq 0$, where $c_i$ are the Clifford generators for the Clifford algebra the action of $\langle M_1,\ldots ,M_n \rangle$ on $U$ factors through the Clifford algebra of rank $\# \{\alpha_i \neq 0\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Rescale the anti-commuting M_i with nonzero square to Clifford generators.

nodes.name: Decomposition of tau~_lambda into eigenspaces U_alpha
nodes.statement: Let $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ be the genuine irreducible supermodule of $\tilde{S}_n$, associated to $\lambda$. Then the common eigenspaces for $M_i^2$ are labelled by the spectrum data $\alpha \in \mathrm{Sspec}(n,\lambda)$. Hence, when considered as a $\langle M_1,\ldots ,M_n \rangle$-supermodule, $$\tilde{\tau}_\lambda = \bigoplus_{\alpha \in \mathrm{Sspec}(n,\lambda)} U_\alpha.$$
assumptions: Let $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ be the genuine irreducible supermodule of $\tilde{S}_n$, associated to $\lambda$.
nodes.label: JMsummand

nodes.name: tau_i moves eigenspace U_alpha to U_{s_i(alpha)}
nodes.statement: Using the decomposition in Corollary \ref{JMsummand}, the subspace $(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} ) U_\alpha$ of $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ is fixed by $\langle M_j \rangle$ and $$\left(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} \right) U_\alpha =U_{s_i(\alpha)}.$$
nodes.statement_short: The corrected operator tau_i - (M_i - M_{i+1})/(q(a_i)-q(a_{i+1})) maps U_alpha onto U_{s_i(alpha)}.
nodes.label: negative

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.4
nodes.statement: One can see that for every $u \in U_\alpha$, $$M_j \left(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} \right)u = - \left(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} \right) M_{s_i(j)}u.$$ Therefore we can conclude that $\left(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} \right) U_\alpha$ is the subspace we labelled $U_{s_i(\alpha)}$. Note that if $s_i(\alpha) \notin \mathrm{Sspec}(n,\lambda)$ then $\left(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} \right) U_\alpha = 0$ hence, in this case, $\tau_i = \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})}$ on $U_\alpha$.
nodes.statement_short: Commute M_j past the corrected operator, which intertwines M_j with M_{s_i(j)}.

nodes.name: Isomorphism P_{s_i}
nodes.statement: If $\alpha$ and $s_i(\alpha)$ are in $\mathrm{Sspec}(n,\lambda)$ then define $P_{s_i}:V_\alpha \to V_{s_i(\alpha)}$ to be the vector space isomorphism such that $$M_{s_i(j)}^2 (P_{s_i} (v)) = P_{s_i} M_j v \text{ for all } v \in V_\alpha.$$

nodes.name: Action of tau_i on V_lambda
nodes.statement: Let $V_\lambda = \sum_{\alpha \in \mathrm{Sspec}(n, \lambda)} V_\alpha$ as supermodules of $\langle M_1,\ldots ,M_n\rangle \subset \tilde{S}_n$. Let $\alpha = (\alpha_1,\ldots ,\alpha_n) \in \mathrm{Sspec}(n, \lambda)$. The action of $\tau_i$, on $V_\alpha$ is defined in the following way. If $s_i(\alpha) \in \mathrm{Sspec}(n)$ then, $$\tau_i = \frac{M_i - M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) -q(a_{i+1})}- \left(1 - \frac{q(a_i) +q(a_{i+1})}{(q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1}))^2}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}} P_{s_i} .$$ If $s_i(\alpha ) \notin \mathrm{Sspec}(n, \lambda)$ then $(1 - \frac{q(a_i) +q(a_{i+1})}{(q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})^2}))= 0$ and on $V_\alpha$, $$\tau_i = \frac{M_i - M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) -q(a_{i+1})}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Defines V_lambda as a sum of V_alpha over Sspec(n, lambda) with tau_i acting by an explicit Jucys-Murphy expression plus a multiple of P_{s_i}.
nodes.label: actionoftau

nodes.name: Explicit model of the irreducible genuine projective supermodules
nodes.statement: For the set of shifted tableaux $\mathcal{SP}(n)$, $\{V_\lambda: \lambda \in \mathcal{SP}(n)\}$ is a full set of representatives of the irreducible genuine projective supermodules of $\tilde{S}_n$.
conclusions: $\{V_\lambda: \lambda \in \mathcal{SP}(n)\}$ is a full set of representatives of the irreducible genuine projective supermodules of $\tilde{S}_n$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6.7
nodes.statement: All we need to show is that the supermodules $V_\lambda$ are isomorphic to $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$. Corollary \ref{JMsummand} shows that they are isomorphic as $\langle M_1,\ldots,M_n\rangle$-supermodules. The following arguments will show that the action of $\tau_i$ agree on both $V_\lambda$ and $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$. If $s_i(\alpha) \notin \mathrm{Sspec}(n,\lambda)$ then Lemma \ref{negative} shows that $\tau_i$ acts on both supermodules identically. In the case that $(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} )$ interchanges $V_\alpha$ and $S_{s_i(\alpha)}$ one observes, that applying this operator twice gives $$\left(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})}\right) ^2 = \left(1 - \frac{q(a_i) +q(a_{i+1})}{(q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})^2})\right)Id$$ on $V_\alpha$. Let $p = 1 - \frac{q(a_i) +q(a_{i+1})}{(q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1}))^2} $. Furthermore, again by Lemma \ref{negative} $$\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{p}} P_{s_i}. $$ Rearranging this equation gives the result, $$\tau_i = \frac{M_i - M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) -q(a_{i+1})}- \left(1 - \frac{q(a_i) +q(a_{i+1})}{(q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1}))^2}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}} P_{s_i} .$$ So again the action of $\tau_i$ is identical on both modules.
nodes.statement_short: Compare with tau~_lambda: same Jucys-Murphy decomposition, and Lemma 6.4 forces the same tau_i action in both cases.

nodes.name: Hook length formula for shifted tableaux
nodes.statement: \cite[1.2]{S80} The hook length formula for shifted tableaux gives an explicit description for the number of standard shifted tableaux for a shifted partition $\lambda = (\lambda_1,\ldots ,\lambda_r\} \vDash n$, $$\# \{\text{ standard shifted tableaux of shape }\lambda\} = \frac{n!}{\lambda_1!\ldots \lambda_r!} \prod_{i=1}^{r} \frac{\lambda_i - \lambda_j}{\lambda_i +\lambda_j}.$$

nodes.name: Dimension of V_lambda
nodes.statement: The dimension of $V_\lambda$ is $$2^{\lceil \frac{n-l(\lambda)}{2}\rceil} \frac{n!}{\lambda_1!\ldots \lambda_r!} \Pi_{i=1}^{r} \frac{\lambda_i - \lambda_j}{\lambda_i +\lambda_j}.$$
nodes.statement_short: dim V_lambda = 2^{ceil((n-l)/2)} times the number of standard shifted tableaux of shape lambda.
nodes.label: dimension

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 6.9
nodes.statement: We built $V_\lambda$ as a direct sum of simple supermodules $\mathcal{S}_{n-l(\lambda)}$, which have dimension $2^{\lceil \frac{n-l(\lambda)}{2}\rceil}$. The number of $\mathcal{S}_{n-l(\lambda)}$ in the sum is equal to the number of standard shifted tableaux, which is $\frac{n!}{\lambda_1!\ldots \lambda_r!} \prod_{i=1}^{r} \frac{\lambda_i - \lambda_j}{\lambda_i +\lambda_j}$.
nodes.statement_short: Count spinor summands by the shifted hook length formula.

nodes.name: Dimension of the ungraded representations sigma~_lambda
nodes.statement: Corollary \ref{dimension} shows that the ungraded representations $\tilde{\sigma}_\lambda$ in \cite{CH15} have dimension $$ 2^{\lfloor \frac{n-l(\lambda)}{2}\rfloor} \frac{n!}{\lambda_1!\ldots \lambda_r!} \prod_{i=1}^{r} \frac{\lambda_i - \lambda_j}{\lambda_i +\lambda_j}.$$
nodes.statement_short: The ungraded modules of [CH15] have dimension 2^{floor((n-l)/2)} times the shifted tableaux count.

nodes.name: Explicit model of V_(3,1) for S~_4
nodes.statement: Take $\tilde{S}_4$ and the shifted tableau $\lambda = (3,1) = \young(\hfil \hfil \hfil ,:\hfil ).$ There are two standard shifted tableaux, namely, $$\young(123,:4) \hspace{5mm} \young(124,:3) .$$ with content vectors $$\alpha_1 = (0,1,2,0), \alpha_2= (0,1,0,2).$$ In this case $n - l(\lambda) = 2$ so our building blocks are $C(2)$-supermodules. Let $\mathcal{S}$ be the (1,1) dimensional supermodule of $C(2) = \langle c_1 , c_2 : c_1c_2 = -c_2c_1 , c_i^2 =1\rangle$ where $$c_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 &0\end{bmatrix} \text{ and } c_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \sqrt{-1} \\ -\sqrt{-1} &0\end{bmatrix}.$$ As a superspace $V_{(3,1)} =\mathcal{S}^1 \oplus \mathcal{S}^2$, where $\mathcal{S}^j \cong \mathcal{S}$ as a $C(2)$-module. For the action of the Jucys-Murphy elements, $M_1= 0$, $M_2 = (\sqrt{2}c_1,\sqrt{2} c_1)$, $M_3 = (\sqrt{6}c_2,0)$ and $M_4 = (0,\sqrt{6}c_2)$. Finally, to calculate the action of $\tau_i$, since $s_i(\alpha_j) \in \mathrm{Sspec}(4, (3,1)) $ for $i = 1,2,$ then $\tau_1$ and $ \tau_2$ fix $\mathcal{S}^1$ and $\mathcal{S}^2$. Explicitly, using Definition \ref{actionoftau}: $$\tau_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \sqrt{2} & 0 & 0 \\ \sqrt{2} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2} & 0 \end{bmatrix},$$ $$\tau_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{-6} - \sqrt{2}) & 0 & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{-6}+\sqrt{2}) & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2} & 0 \end{bmatrix}.$$ Now $\tau_3$ interchanges $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$, hence again using Theorem \ref{actionoftau} $$\tau_3 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \frac{\sqrt{-6}}{3} & \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} & 0 \\ - \frac{\sqrt{-6}}{3} & 0 & 0 & \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \\ \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} & 0 & 0 & \frac{\sqrt{-6}}{3} \\ 0 & \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} & - \frac{\sqrt{-6}}{3} & 0 \end{bmatrix}.$$ This gives an explicit realisation of of the supermodule $V_{(3,1)}$ on the four dimensional space spanned by $\{v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4\}$, by the above matrices. Although note that the even space is $V_{(3,1)}^0 = span\{v_1,v_4\}$ and the odd space is $V_{(3,1)}^1 = span\{v_2,v_3\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Matrices for the Jucys-Murphy elements and tau_1, tau_2, tau_3 on the 4-dimensional supermodule V_(3,1).

nodes.name: Vogan's morphism
nodes.statement: Vogan's morphism for graded Hecke algebras is the algebra homomorphism $\zeta: Z(\mathbb{H}) \to Z(\mathbb{C}[\tilde{S}_n])$ defined such that $\zeta(z)$ for $z \in Z(\mathbb{H})$ is the unique element in $Z(\tilde{S}_n)$ such that $$z\otimes 1 = \rho (\zeta(z)) + Da + aD$$ as elements of $\mathbb{H} \otimes C(V)$, for some $a \in \mathbb{H}\otimes C(V)$.

nodes.name: Projected Vogan morphism
nodes.statement: We will describe $$\underline{\zeta}: Z(\mathbb{H}) \to Z(\mathcal{T}_n).$$ This is $\zeta$ composed with the projection from $\mathbb{C}[\tilde{S}_n]$ to $\mathcal{T}_n$.

nodes.name: Central elements are detected by irreducible representations
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a semisimple finite dimensional $\mathbb{C}$-algebra and let $a$ and $b \in Z(A)$. Suppose for all irreducible representations $\sigma$ of $A$, $$\sigma(a)=\sigma(b),$$ then $a = b$.
assumptions: Let $A$ be a semisimple finite dimensional $\mathbb{C}$-algebra and let $a$ and $b \in Z(A)$.
Suppose for all irreducible representations $\sigma$ of $A$, $$\sigma(a)=\sigma(b),$$
nodes.label: density

nodes.name: Element nu_lambda defining chi_lambda
nodes.statement: Let $\{y_i\}$ be a dual basis of $\{x_i\}$ then the element defining $\chi_\lambda$ is $$\nu_\lambda = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^k \sum_{j =1}^{\lambda_i} (-\lambda_i +2j-1)y_{\lambda_{i+1}+j}.$$

nodes.name: Coefficients of nu for lambda = (5,3,2)
Dual map zeta*
nodes.statement: The dual map $\underline{\zeta}^*$ takes the irreducible representations of $\mathcal{T}_n$ to central characters of $\mathbb{H}$. Let $\sigma \in \mathrm{irr}(\mathcal{T}_n)$ and let $p \in Z(\mathbb{H})$. The central character $\underline{\zeta}^* (\sigma): Z(\mathbb{H}) \to \mathbb{C}$ is $$ \underline{\zeta}^*(\sigma)(f) = \sigma(\underline{\zeta}(p)).$$

nodes.name: zeta* sends V_lambda to chi_lambda
nodes.statement: Let $(V_\lambda,\sigma_\lambda)$ be the$\mathcal{T}_n$ representation described in Section \ref{explicit} corresponding to a strict partition $\lambda$, let $\chi_\lambda$ be the central character of $X_\lambda$. Then as described $$\underline{\zeta}^* (V_\lambda) = \chi_\lambda.$$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 7.4
nodes.statement: This is a corollary of \cite[4.4]{BCT12}.
nodes.statement_short: Corollary of [BCT12, 4.4].

nodes.name: Criterion for computing the projected Vogan morphism
nodes.statement: Let $P_{\mathbb{H}} \in Z(\mathbb{H})$ and $P_{\mathcal{T}_n} \in Z(\mathcal{T}_n)$. If, for all $\lambda$ strict, $$V_\lambda(P_{\mathcal{T}_n}) = \chi_\lambda(P_\mathbb{H})$$ then $\underline{\zeta}(P_\mathbb{H}) = P_{\mathcal{T}_n}.$
assumptions: Let $P_{\mathbb{H}} \in Z(\mathbb{H})$ and $P_{\mathcal{T}_n} \in Z(\mathcal{T}_n)$.
nodes.label: equivalent

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 7.5
nodes.statement: The set of $V_\lambda$ for shifted partitions is a full set of irreducible representations of $\mathcal{T}_n$. Also $\underline{\zeta}^*(V_\lambda) = \chi_\lambda$. So the assumption is equivalent to, for all $\sigma \in \mathrm{irr}(\mathcal{T}_n)$, $\sigma(P_{\mathcal{T}_n}) =(\sigma)(\underline{\zeta}(P_{\mathbb{H}})).$ Then applying Lemma \ref{density}, $\underline{\zeta}(P_{\mathbb{H}}) = P_{\mathcal{T}_n}$.
nodes.statement_short: The V_lambda exhaust irr(T_n) and zeta*(V_lambda) = chi_lambda; conclude by Lemma 7.1.

nodes.name: Power sums P_T^{2m} and P_H^{2m}
nodes.statement: Let $M_i$ be the Jucys-Murphy elements for $\mathcal{T}_n$. We define, $$P_{\mathcal{T}_n}^{2m} = \sum_{i=1}^n (2M_i)^{2m} \in Z(\mathcal{T}_n)_{\mathrm{even}}.$$ The set $\{\xi_1,..,\xi_n\}$ is an orthogonal basis of $V$. Define $$P_{\mathbb{H}}^{2m} = \sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor \frac{m}{2} \rfloor} {{m}\choose{2j}} \sum_{i=1}^n (2x_i)^{2m-2j}\in Z(\mathbb{H})_{\mathrm{even}}.$$

nodes.name: Power sums act identically
nodes.statement: For $m, n\in \mathbb{N}$ and for all shifted $\lambda$, $$\sigma_\lambda(P_{\mathcal{T}_n}^{2m}) = \chi_\lambda(P_{\mathbb{H}}^{2m}).$$
assumptions: For $m, n\in \mathbb{N}$ and for all shifted $\lambda$
nodes.label: action

nodes.name: Vogan morphism on even power sums
nodes.statement: We have $$\underline{\zeta}(P_{\mathbb{H}}^{2m}) = P_{\mathcal{T}_n}^{2m}.$$

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 7.8
nodes.statement: This follows from Lemma \ref{equivalent} and Theorem \ref{action}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine Lemma 7.5 with Theorem 7.7.

nodes.name: Odd power sums vanish under chi_lambda
nodes.statement: For all $\lambda$ strict and $n,m \in \mathbb{N}$, $$\chi_\lambda(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^{2m+1} )= 0.$$
assumptions: For all $\lambda$ strict and $n,m \in \mathbb{N}$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 7.9
nodes.statement: The character $\chi_\lambda$ is defined by $\nu_\lambda$ which for every positive coefficient has a negative coefficient of the same magnitude. Hence any symmetric odd polynomial evaluated on $\nu_\lambda$ is zero.
nodes.statement_short: nu_lambda is symmetric under negation, so odd symmetric polynomials vanish on it.

nodes.name: Image and kernel of the projected Vogan morphism
nodes.statement: The map $\underline{\zeta}$ surjects onto the even part of the centre of $\mathcal{T}_n$. Also $\ker(\underline{\zeta}) \supset S(V)_{\mathrm{odd}}$.
also_stated_at: Vogan's map projected onto the group algebra $\mathcal{T}_n \cong \tilde{S}_n/ \langle z +1 \rangle$, $\underline{\zeta}: Z(\mathbb{H}) \to Z[\mathcal{T}_n]$, is surjective onto the even part of the centre. Also $\underline{\zeta}$ kills all odd polynomials in $Z(\mathbb{H})$.
conclusions: The map $\underline{\zeta}$ surjects onto the even part of the centre of $\mathcal{T}_n$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 7.10
nodes.statement: The first statement is clear since $Z(\mathcal{T})_{\mathrm{even}}$ is generated by the symmetric polynomials in the squares of the Jucys-Murphy elements. The second statement follows from the fact that every symmetric homogeneous polynomial of odd degree is generated by monomials of power polynomials where there is at least one odd power polynomial. Hence $\underline{\zeta}$, since it is a homomorphism, will kill any homogeneous symmetric polynomial of odd degree.
nodes.statement_short: Even centre is generated by symmetric polynomials in M_i^2; odd symmetric polynomials involve an odd power sum, which is killed.

nodes.name: Brundan-Kleshchev basis of the even centre
nodes.statement: Note that Kleschev and Brundan \cite[3.2]{BK01} provide a basis for $Z(\mathcal{T}_n)_{\mathrm{even}}$ in the form of products of power polynomials of the $M_i^2$. The set $\{ \Pi_{i=1}^{k} P_{\mathcal{T}_n}^{2m_i} : \sum_{i=1}^{k}2m_i+1 \leq n\}$ is a basis for $Z(\mathcal{T}_n)_{\mathrm{even}}$.

nodes.name: Basis of the centre from images of P_H
nodes.statement: Therefore $$\{ \underline{\zeta}'(\Pi_{i=1}^{k} P_{\mathbb{H}}^{2m_i}) : \sum_{i=1}^{k}2m_i +1 \leq n\}$$ is a basis of $Z(\mathcal{T}_n)$.

nodes.name: Partitions of length one P^1
nodes.statement: Define $\mathcal{P}^1$ to be the set of partitions, of any number, of length 1. $\mathcal{P}^1_n$ is the singleton subset of $\mathcal{P}^1$, consisting of the partition $\lambda = (n).$

nodes.name: Theorem 7.7 for partitions of length one
nodes.statement: Let $\mu \in \mathcal{P}^1$ be a partition of length one then, for all $m \in \mathbb{N}$, $$\sigma_\mu(P_{\mathcal{T}_n}^{2m}) = \chi_\mu (P_{\mathbb{H}}^{2m}).$$
assumptions: Let $\mu \in \mathcal{P}^1$ be a partition of length one
nodes.label: action2

nodes.name: Reduction to partitions of length one
nodes.statement: Theorem \ref{action2} implies Theorem \ref{action}, that is, it is enough to show the result on modules corresponding to the partition of length one.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 7.13
nodes.statement: Let $\lambda = (\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\ldots ,\lambda_k)$ be a shifted partition. We are studying the action of power polynomials. Let $Q_{\mathbb{H}}^j$ be the $j^{th}$ power polynomial in the $x_i$'s, $\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^j$. Let $\chi_{\lambda_1 \times \ldots \times \lambda_k}$ be the central character of the $\mathbb{H}_{\lambda_1} \times \ldots \times \mathbb{H}_{\lambda_k}$-module $St_{\lambda_1} \otimes \ldots \otimes St_{\lambda_k}$ and $\chi_{\lambda_l}$ be the central character of the $\mathbb{H}_{\lambda_l}$-module $St_{\lambda_l}$. We consider $\mathbb{H}_{\lambda_l}$ to be embedded in $\mathbb{H}$ such that $x_{\lambda_{l-1}+1}, \ldots, x_{\lambda_l}$ are in the image of $\mathbb{H}_{\lambda_l}$. Since $Q_{\mathbb{H}}^j \in \mathbb{H}_{\lambda_1} \times \ldots \times \mathbb{H}_{\lambda_k}$, then $$\chi_\lambda(Q_\mathbb{H}^j) = \chi_{\lambda_1 \times \ldots \times \lambda_k}(Q_\mathbb{H}^j) = \sum_{l=1}^k \chi_{\lambda_l} (Q_{\mathbb{H}_{\lambda_l}}^j).$$ Similarly, for $Q_{\mathcal{T}_n}^j = \sum_{i=1}^n M_i^j$, $$\sigma_\lambda (Q_{\mathcal{T}_n}^j) = \sum_{l=1}^k \sigma_{\lambda_l}(Q_{\mathcal{T}_{\lambda_l}}^j).$$ Therefore if we can prove the result of the theorem for every $\mu = (\lambda_l) \in \mathcal{P}^1$, then using the above decomposition of both $\chi_\lambda(Q_\mathbb{H}^j)$ and $\sigma_\lambda (Q_{\mathcal{T}_n}^j)$ we can extend this to $\sigma_{\lambda}$ and $\chi_\lambda$ for every strict $\lambda$.
nodes.statement_short: Both power-sum actions decompose additively over the parts lambda_l of lambda.

nodes.name: Power sums of Jucys-Murphy elements via contents
nodes.statement: Let $\lambda = (\lambda_1,..,\lambda_n) \Vdash n$ be a shifted partition, with associated shifted Young diagram $\lambda = \{(i,j) : i = 1,..,l(\lambda) \text{ and } j = i -1 ,\ldots ,i -1+ \lambda_i. \}$. Then $$\sigma_\lambda(P_{\mathcal{T}_n}^{2m}) =\sigma_\lambda(\sum_{i=1}^n (2M_i)^{2m}) = \sum_{i=1}^n (cont(i))^m(cont(i)+1)^m.$$
nodes.label: cont

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 7.14
nodes.statement: This is a restatement of Theorem \ref{spectrumdata} where we described the action of $M_i^2$ on $V_\lambda$. Recall that the result showed that on a certain subspace $M_i^2$ acted by $cont(i)(cont(i)+1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Restatement of Theorem 5.13.

nodes.name: Action of P_T on the length-one partition (t)
nodes.statement: Fix a $t\in \mathbb{Z}$ and let $\mu = (\mu_i) = (t) \Vdash t$. Then $$\sigma_\mu(\sum_{i=1}^t (2M_i)^{2m}) = \sum_{i=1}^t (i-1)^m(i)^m.$$
nodes.label: actionT

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 7.15
nodes.statement: This follows from Lemma \ref{cont} since for $\mu$, $\mathrm{cont}(i) = i-1$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 7.14 with cont(i) = i-1.

nodes.name: Action of P_H on the length-one partition (t)
nodes.statement: Fix a $t \in \mathbb{Z}$ Let $\mu = (\mu_1)= (t) = \Vdash t$. Then $$\chi_\mu (\sum_{i=1}^t (2x_i)^{2m} ) = \sum_{i=1}^{t} (2(i-1)-(t-1))^{2m}.$$
nodes.label: actionH

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 7.16
nodes.statement: The central character $\chi_\mu$ is defined by $\nu_\mu = \sum_{i=1}^{t} (2(i-1) - (t-1)y_i$. The result follows by evaluating $\sum_{i=1}^t (2x_i)^{2m}$ at $\nu_\mu$.
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate the power sum at nu_mu.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 7.12
nodes.statement: Fix $m \in \mathbb{N}$. We prove this statement by induction on $n$ with steps of length two. Note that for $n=0$ and $n=1$, all operators act by zero, hence the base cases are trivial. Suppose the result is true for $n-2$, so: $$\sigma_{(n-2)}(P_{\mathcal{T}_{n-2}}^{2m}) = \chi_{(n-2)} (P_{\mathbb{H}}^{2m}).$$ Now, considering that $\sigma_{(n-2)}$ is the restriction of $\sigma_{(n)}$ to $\mathcal{T}_{n-2}$, $$\sigma_{(n)}(P_{\mathcal{T}_{n}}^{2m}) - \sigma_{(n-2)}(P_{\mathcal{T}_{n-2}}^{2m}) = \sigma_{(n)}( (2M_{n-1})^{2m} + (2M_{n})^{2m}).$$ By Corollary \ref{actionT} this is equal to \begin{equation*} \begin{split} \sum_{i=1}^{t} (i-1)^m(i)^m - \sum_{i=1}^{t-2} (i-1)^m(i)^m & = (t-2)^m(t-1)^m + (t-1)^m(t)^m\\ & = (t-1)^m ((t-1 + 1)^m + (t-1 -1 )^m ) \\ &= (t-1)^m (\sum_{l=0}^m {m\choose l} (t-1)^{m-l} (1^l + (-1)^l))\\ & = (t-1)^m\sum_{\substack{l \in {0,\ldots ,m} \\\text{ and even} }} 2 {m\choose l} (t-1)^{m-l}\\ & = \sum_{j = 0}^{\lfloor \frac{m}{2} \rfloor} 2 {m \choose 2j} (t-1)^{2m-2j}. \end{split} \end{equation*} We know that $$\chi_{(t)}(P_{\mathbb{H}_t}^{2m}) - \chi_{(t-2)}P_{\mathbb{H}_{t-2}}^{2m},$$ is just the action of the $x_{t}$ and $x_{t-1}$. Expanding out $P_{\mathbb{H}_t}^{2m}$ and explicitly writing $\chi_{(t)}(P_{\mathbb{H}_t}^{2m})$ using Lemma \ref{actionH}, we know that $$\chi_{(t)}(P_{\mathbb{H}_t}^{2m}) - \chi_{(t-2)}P_{\mathbb{H}_{t-2}}^{2m}= \sum_{j = 0}^{\lfloor \frac{m}{2} \rfloor} 2 {m \choose 2j} (t-1)^{2m-2j}.$$ Therefore we have shown that the inductive step holds. Hence $$\sigma_{(n)}(P_{\mathcal{T}_{n-2}}^{2m}) = \chi_{(n)} (P_{\mathbb{H}}^{2m})$$ by induction.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on n in steps of two. The difference of consecutive cases reduces both sides to the same binomial sum.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 7.7
nodes.statement: We have proved Theorem \ref{action2} and hence have proved Theorem \ref{action}.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 7.12 together with Lemma 7.13.

nodes.name: Match column a_i removal with row i removal
nodes.statement: Because $\lambda$ is strict, the column of $\lambda$ which is first larger than $i$, $\lambda_{a_i}'$, will always be the column that has a block from $\lambda_1,\ldots ,\lambda_i$ and no others. So removing a block from row $\lambda_i$ is equivalent to removing a block from column $\lambda_{a_i}'$.
nodes.statement_short: Match column a_i removal with row i removal

nodes.name: Conclude the formula for lambda^(i)
nodes.statement: Hence $\lambda^{(i)} = (\lambda_1,\ldots ,\lambda_{i-1},\lambda_{i} -1 , \lambda_{i+1},\ldots ,\lambda_r)$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude the formula for lambda^(i)

nodes.name: Deduce equality with Theta
nodes.statement: The second statement follows since we have an explicit description of $\{\lambda^{(i)} : i =1,\ldots ,l(\lambda) \}$.
nodes.statement_short: Deduce equality with Theta

nodes.name: Reverse grading and apply Garsia-Procesi branching
nodes.statement: By Remark \ref{reverse} one can write $\chi_\textbf{q}(\lambda) = p^\lambda (\boldsymbol{\frac{1}{q}}) q^{n(\lambda)}$. Then, we can use the restriction rules given by Theorem \ref{GPbranching} to restrict $\chi_\textbf{q}(\lambda)$ in terms of the characters $p^{\lambda^{(i)}}(\textbf{q})$. Remark \ref{reverse} can be used again to rewrite this in terms of characters $\chi_{\textbf{q}}(\lambda^{(i)})$.
nodes.statement_short: Reverse grading and apply Garsia-Procesi branching

nodes.name: Compute the exponent via n(lambda)
nodes.statement: The coefficient one gets is $\textbf{q}^{i-1+ n(\lambda) - n(\lambda^{(i)})}$. Writing out the definition of $n(\lambda)$; $$n(\lambda) - n(\lambda^{(i)}) = \sum_{j=1}^l(\lambda)(j-1)\lambda_j - \sum_{j=1}^{l(\lambda^{(i)})} (j-1)\lambda^{(i)}_j.$$
nodes.statement_short: Compute the exponent via n(lambda)

nodes.name: Lemma 4.3: lambda^(i) differs in entry i
nodes.statement: However, by Lemma \ref{strictset}, $\lambda$ and $\lambda^{(i)}$ differ by only one entry for $\lambda$ strict. This difference is in the $ith$ entry.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 4.3: lambda^(i) differs in entry i

nodes.name: Exponent equals 2i-2
nodes.statement: Therefore $n(\lambda)$ and $n(\lambda^{(i)})$ differ by $i-1$. Hence $i-1+ n(\lambda) - n(\lambda^{(i)}) = 2i-2$.
nodes.statement_short: Exponent equals 2i-2

nodes.name: Write tau~ via X_{-1} and the spinor
nodes.statement: We note that $a_\lambda \tilde{\tau}_\lambda = X_{-1}(\lambda) \otimes \mathcal{S}$. Here, $\mathcal{S}$ (resp. $\mathcal{S}'$) is the spinor supermodule for the Clifford algebra $C(n)$ (resp. $C(n-1)$).
nodes.statement_short: Write tau~ via X_{-1} and the spinor

nodes.name: Restrict both factors separately
nodes.statement: Hence restricting $a_\lambda \tilde{\tau_\lambda} $ to $\tilde{S}_{n-1}$ is equivalent to restricting $X_{-1}(\lambda)$ to $S_{n-1}$ and $\mathcal{S}$ to $C(n-1)$. Therefore $$a_\lambda Res^{n}_{n-1} \tilde{\tau}_\lambda = Res^{n}_{n-1}\mathcal{S} \otimes Res^{n}_{n-1} X_{-1}(\lambda) $$ $$= c \mathcal{S}' \otimes \bigoplus_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)} X_{-1}(\lambda^{(i)}).$$ $$= \bigoplus_{{\lambda^{(i)}} \text{ which are strict }} c\mathcal{S}' \otimes X_{-1}(\lambda^{(i)}).$$ Here, $c \in \mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}$ and will be determined in Theorem \ref{branchingrules}.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict both factors separately

nodes.name: Strict lambda^(i) occur
nodes.statement: Hence, for every strict $\lambda^{(i)}$ the $\tilde{S}_n$ supermodule $\tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(i)}}$ occurs as a summand.
nodes.statement_short: Strict lambda^(i) occur

nodes.name: Reduce to computing multiplicities
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{summands} we already know which summands will occur. Hence calculating the multiplicities is all that is required.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to computing multiplicities

nodes.name: Multiplicities for spinor and X_{-1}
nodes.statement: We know the multiplicities of the restriction of the spinor $S_n$; $2$ if $n$ is even, $1$ otherwise. Also, by Lemma \ref{summands} the multiplicities in the restriction of $X_{-1}(\lambda)$ are always $1$.
nodes.statement_short: Multiplicities for spinor and X_{-1}

nodes.name: Compare a_lambda over eight cases
nodes.statement: Hence, we can find the multiplicities for $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ by comparing $\frac{1}{a_\lambda}$ and $\frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}}$ from Proposition \ref{alambda}. This is a simple calculation on the eight cases $$\frac{1}{a_\lambda} = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2} \frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ even, } l(\lambda) \text{ even and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda),\\ \frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ even, } l(\lambda) \text{ even and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda)-1,\\ \frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ even, } l(\lambda) \text{ odd and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda),\\ \frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ even, } l(\lambda) \text{ odd and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda)-1,\\ 2\frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}}& n \text{ odd, } l(\lambda) \text{ even and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda),\\ \frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ odd, } l(\lambda) \text{ even and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda)-1,\\ \frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ odd, } l(\lambda) \text{ odd and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda),\\ \frac{1}{a_{\lambda^{(i)}}} & n \text{ odd, } l(\lambda) \text{ odd and } l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda)-1.\\ \end{cases}$$
nodes.statement_short: Compare a_lambda over eight cases

nodes.name: Only lambda^(r) can be shorter
nodes.statement: Note that $l(\lambda^{(i)}) = l(\lambda)-1$ occurs once if and only if $\lambda_r = 1$, in which case it is the partition $\lambda^{(r)}$ which has shorter length.
nodes.statement_short: Only lambda^(r) can be shorter

nodes.name: First part via X_lambda and Lemma 5.10
nodes.statement: The first part can be proved by noticing that, when one forgets the grading, the module $X_{-1}(\lambda)$ is just the parabolically induced module $X_\lambda$, see \cite{BM83}. Hence, one can use Lemma \ref{HOmega} to show how $\Omega_\mathbb{H}$ acts. The constant $( \nu, \nu )$ is exactly the sum we stated.
nodes.statement_short: First part via X_lambda and Lemma 5.10

nodes.name: Second part by induction on row sums
nodes.statement: The second part follows by a simple induction. One can show $\sum_{j=1}^{\lambda_i} (2j - \lambda_i)^2= \sum_{j=1}^{\lambda_i} j(j+1) = \sum_{j=1}^{\lambda_k} q(\mathrm{cont}(k,j))$, splitting the cases when $\lambda_i$ is odd or even. This will be covered in more detail in Section \ref{vogan}.
nodes.statement_short: Second part by induction on row sums

nodes.name: Chain of equalities for the Casimir
nodes.statement: $$\Omega_{\tilde{S}_n}= \frac{1}{4}\sum_{\substack{\alpha,\beta\in\Phi^+ \\ s_\alpha(\beta)<0}} |\alpha||\beta|\tau_\alpha \tau_\beta $$ $$=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{\alpha,\beta\in \Phi^+} |\alpha||\beta|\tau_\alpha \tau_\beta= \frac{1}{4}(\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}|\alpha|\tau_\alpha)^2$$ $$=\frac{1}{4} (\sum_{k=1}^{n}|\alpha|M_k)^2= \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^n M_k^2$$
nodes.statement_short: Chain of equalities for the Casimir

nodes.name: Justify second equality
nodes.statement: In the second equality, we use $\tau_\alpha \tau_\beta = - \tau_\beta \tau_{s_\alpha(\beta)}$ for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ such that $s_\alpha(\beta)>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Justify second equality

nodes.name: Justify last equalities by anti-commutation
nodes.statement: The third equality uses the fact that every $\sum_{i=1}^n M_k = \sum_{\alpha \in \Phi^+} \tau_\alpha$ and the last equality uses the fact that the Jucys-Murphy elements anti-commute in $\mathcal{T}_n$ \cite[3.1]{BK01}. Hence the square of the sum is equal to the sum of the squares.
nodes.statement_short: Justify last equalities by anti-commutation

nodes.name: Set up induction and fix lambda
nodes.statement: We prove the theorem by induction, the base case being trivial. Suppose for every shifted partition $\mu \in \mathcal{SP}(n-1)$, $\mathrm{Scont}(n-1, \mu) = \mathrm{Sspec}(n-1, \mu)$. Let us fix a shifted partition $\lambda$ of $n$, and consider $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ the irreducible representation of $\mathcal{T}_n$ associated to $\lambda$.
nodes.statement_short: Set up induction and fix lambda

nodes.name: Take alpha in Sspec and eigenvector v_alpha
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha = (\alpha_1,\ldots ,\alpha_n)\in \mathrm{Sspec}(n , \lambda)$. By definition there exists a vector $v_\alpha \in \tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ such that $M_j^2(v_\alpha) =q(\alpha_j )v_\alpha \text{ for all } $j$.$
nodes.statement_short: Take alpha in Sspec and eigenvector v_alpha

nodes.name: Branching and induction hypothesis
nodes.statement: The restriction of $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ to $\mathcal{T}_{n-1}$ is the direct sum, $\bigoplus_{i =1}^{l(\lambda)} \tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(i)}}$. Also $v_\alpha$ is an eigenvector for the Jucys-Murphys elements. Hence $v_\alpha \in \tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(j)}} \subset \tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ for some fixed $j$. We know, by the inductive hypothesis, $(\alpha_1,\ldots ,\alpha_{n-1}) \in \mathrm{Sspec}(n-1,\lambda^{(j)}) = \mathrm{Scont}(n-1,\lambda^{(j)})$. Explicitly, this means there exists a standard numbering $[[\lambda^{(j)}]]$ of $\lambda^{(j)}$ which corresponds to $(\alpha_1,\ldots ,\alpha_{n-1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Branching and induction hypothesis

nodes.name: Casimir actions on v_alpha for n and n-1
nodes.statement: Now using Lemma \ref{content}, Lemma \ref{squares} and Theorem \ref{Dirac}, we can describe the action of the Casimir elements of $\tilde{S}_n$ and $\tilde{S}_{n-1}$ on $v_\alpha$. Since $v_\alpha$ is in $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ , $$ \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^n M_k^2 v_\alpha = \Omega_{\tilde{S}_n} v_\alpha= \Omega_{\mathbb{H}_n}v_\alpha =\frac{1}{4} \sum_{(i,j) \in \lambda} \mathrm{cont}(i,j)(\mathrm{cont}(i,j)+1)v_\alpha. $$ However $v_\alpha$ is also contained in $\tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(j)}}\subset \tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ so, $$\frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} M_k^2v_\alpha = \Omega_{\tilde{S}_{n-1}} v_\alpha= \Omega_{\mathbb{H}_{n-1}}v_\alpha =\frac{1}{4} \sum_{(i,j) \in \lambda^{(j)}} \mathrm{cont}(i,j)(\mathrm{cont}(i,j)+1)v_\alpha.$$ the difference of these two Casimir elements is $\frac{1}{2}M_n^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Casimir actions on v_alpha for n and n-1

nodes.name: M_n^2 acts by content of the added box
nodes.statement: Hence $$M_n^2 v_\alpha = \left(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{(i,j) \in \lambda} \mathrm{cont}(i,j)(\mathrm{cont}(i,j)+1) - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{(i,j) \in \lambda^{(j)}} \mathrm{cont}(i,j)(\mathrm{cont}(i,j)+1) \right) v_\alpha$$ $$ =\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{cont}(k,l)(\mathrm{cont}(k,l)+ 1)v_\alpha,$$ where $(k,l)$ is the block of $ \lambda $ not included in $ \lambda^{(i)}.$
nodes.statement_short: M_n^2 acts by content of the added box

nodes.name: alpha is a content vector
nodes.statement: Taking the standard shifted tableau $[[\lambda^{(j)}]]_{(\alpha_1,\ldots ,\alpha_{n-1})}$ associated to $(\alpha_1,\ldots ,\alpha_{n-1})$ and adding the block $(k,l)$ labelled with the number $n$ creates a standard shifted tableau $[[\lambda]]_\alpha$ of shape $\lambda$. By the above argument this standard shifted tableau has content vector equal to $\alpha \in \mathrm{Sspec}(n,\lambda)$. Hence $\alpha \in \mathrm{Scont}(n,\lambda)$.
nodes.statement_short: alpha is a content vector

nodes.name: Reverse direction: take beta in Scont
nodes.statement: For the reverse direction, we use an almost identical argument. Suppose $\beta =(\beta_1,\ldots ,\beta_n) \in \mathrm{Scont}(n,\lambda)$ corresponds to a standard shifted tableau $[[\lambda]]_\beta$.
nodes.statement_short: Reverse direction: take beta in Scont

nodes.name: Induction hypothesis gives eigenvector
nodes.statement: By restriction and inductive hypothesis, there exists a vector $v_{(\beta_1,\ldots ,\beta_{n-1})} \in \tilde{\tau}_{\lambda^{(j)}} \subset \tilde{\tau}_\lambda$ such that $M_k^2 v_{(\beta_1,\ldots ,\beta_{n-1})} = q(\beta_k) v_{(\beta_1,\ldots ,\beta_{n-1})}$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction hypothesis gives eigenvector

nodes.name: M_n^2 eigenvalue gives beta in Sspec
nodes.statement: Again using the fact that $M_n^2$ acts by the difference of the Casimir elements $\Omega_{S_n}$ and $\Omega_{S_{n-1}}$, we get, $$M_n^2 v_{(\beta_1,\ldots ,\beta_{n-1})} = 2(\Omega_{\tilde{S}_n} - \Omega_{\tilde{S}_{n-1}}) = \frac{1}{2}q(\mathrm{cont}(n))v_{(\beta_1,\ldots ,\beta_{n-1})},$$ where $\mathrm{cont}(n)$ is the content of the box labelled by $n$ in $[[\lambda]]_\beta$. Hence $\beta \in Spec(n,\lambda)$.
nodes.statement_short: M_n^2 eigenvalue gives beta in Sspec

nodes.name: Commutation relation with M_j
nodes.statement: One can see that for every $u \in U_\alpha$, $$M_j \left(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} \right)u = - \left(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} \right) M_{s_i(j)}u.$$
nodes.statement_short: Commutation relation with M_j

nodes.name: Image is U_{s_i(alpha)}
nodes.statement: Therefore we can conclude that $\left(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} \right) U_\alpha$ is the subspace we labelled $U_{s_i(\alpha)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Image is U_{s_i(alpha)}

nodes.name: Degenerate case s_i(alpha) not in Sspec
nodes.statement: Note that if $s_i(\alpha) \notin \mathrm{Sspec}(n,\lambda)$ then $\left(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} \right) U_\alpha = 0$ hence, in this case, $\tau_i = \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})}$ on $U_\alpha$.
nodes.statement_short: Degenerate case s_i(alpha) not in Sspec

nodes.name: Reduce to comparing tau_i actions
nodes.statement: All we need to show is that the supermodules $V_\lambda$ are isomorphic to $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$. Corollary \ref{JMsummand} shows that they are isomorphic as $\langle M_1,\ldots,M_n\rangle$-supermodules. The following arguments will show that the action of $\tau_i$ agree on both $V_\lambda$ and $\tilde{\tau}_\lambda$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to comparing tau_i actions

nodes.name: Case s_i(alpha) outside Sspec
nodes.statement: If $s_i(\alpha) \notin \mathrm{Sspec}(n,\lambda)$ then Lemma \ref{negative} shows that $\tau_i$ acts on both supermodules identically.
nodes.statement_short: Case s_i(alpha) outside Sspec

nodes.name: Case where the operator swaps eigenspaces
nodes.statement: In the case that $(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} )$ interchanges $V_\alpha$ and $S_{s_i(\alpha)}$ one observes, that applying this operator twice gives $$\left(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})}\right) ^2 = \left(1 - \frac{q(a_i) +q(a_{i+1})}{(q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})^2})\right)Id$$ on $V_\alpha$. Let $p = 1 - \frac{q(a_i) +q(a_{i+1})}{(q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1}))^2} $. Furthermore, again by Lemma \ref{negative} $$\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{p}} P_{s_i}. $$ Rearranging this equation gives the result, $$\tau_i = \frac{M_i - M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) -q(a_{i+1})}- \left(1 - \frac{q(a_i) +q(a_{i+1})}{(q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1}))^2}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}} P_{s_i} .$$ So again the action of $\tau_i$ is identical on both modules.
nodes.statement_short: Case where the operator swaps eigenspaces

nodes.name: Square of the corrected operator
nodes.statement: In the case that $(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} )$ interchanges $V_\alpha$ and $S_{s_i(\alpha)}$ one observes, that applying this operator twice gives $$\left(\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})}\right) ^2 = \left(1 - \frac{q(a_i) +q(a_{i+1})}{(q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})^2})\right)Id$$ on $V_\alpha$.
nodes.statement_short: Square of the corrected operator

nodes.name: Identify operator with P_{s_i}
nodes.statement: Let $p = 1 - \frac{q(a_i) +q(a_{i+1})}{(q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1}))^2} $. Furthermore, again by Lemma \ref{negative} $$\tau_i - \frac{M_i -M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1})} = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{p}} P_{s_i}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Identify operator with P_{s_i}

nodes.name: Solve for tau_i
nodes.statement: Rearranging this equation gives the result, $$\tau_i = \frac{M_i - M_{i+1}}{q(a_i) -q(a_{i+1})}- \left(1 - \frac{q(a_i) +q(a_{i+1})}{(q(a_i) - q(a_{i+1}))^2}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}} P_{s_i} .$$ So again the action of $\tau_i$ is identical on both modules.
nodes.statement_short: Solve for tau_i

nodes.name: Recall V_lambda exhaust irreps and zeta*
nodes.statement: The set of $V_\lambda$ for shifted partitions is a full set of irreducible representations of $\mathcal{T}_n$. Also $\underline{\zeta}^*(V_\lambda) = \chi_\lambda$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall V_lambda exhaust irreps and zeta*

nodes.name: Reformulate the hypothesis
nodes.statement: So the assumption is equivalent to, for all $\sigma \in \mathrm{irr}(\mathcal{T}_n)$, $\sigma(P_{\mathcal{T}_n}) =(\sigma)(\underline{\zeta}(P_{\mathbb{H}})).$
nodes.statement_short: Reformulate the hypothesis

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 7.1
nodes.statement: Then applying Lemma \ref{density}, $\underline{\zeta}(P_{\mathbb{H}}) = P_{\mathcal{T}_n}$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 7.1

nodes.name: Surjectivity and odd degree structure
nodes.statement: The first statement is clear since $Z(\mathcal{T})_{\mathrm{even}}$ is generated by the symmetric polynomials in the squares of the Jucys-Murphy elements. The second statement follows from the fact that every symmetric homogeneous polynomial of odd degree is generated by monomials of power polynomials where there is at least one odd power polynomial.
nodes.statement_short: Surjectivity and odd degree structure

nodes.name: Homomorphism kills odd polynomials
nodes.statement: Hence $\underline{\zeta}$, since it is a homomorphism, will kill any homogeneous symmetric polynomial of odd degree.
nodes.statement_short: Homomorphism kills odd polynomials

nodes.name: Introduce power sums and component characters
nodes.statement: Let $\lambda = (\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\ldots ,\lambda_k)$ be a shifted partition. We are studying the action of power polynomials. Let $Q_{\mathbb{H}}^j$ be the $j^{th}$ power polynomial in the $x_i$'s, $\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^j$. Let $\chi_{\lambda_1 \times \ldots \times \lambda_k}$ be the central character of the $\mathbb{H}_{\lambda_1} \times \ldots \times \mathbb{H}_{\lambda_k}$-module $St_{\lambda_1} \otimes \ldots \otimes St_{\lambda_k}$ and $\chi_{\lambda_l}$ be the central character of the $\mathbb{H}_{\lambda_l}$-module $St_{\lambda_l}$. We consider $\mathbb{H}_{\lambda_l}$ to be embedded in $\mathbb{H}$ such that $x_{\lambda_{l-1}+1}, \ldots, x_{\lambda_l}$ are in the image of $\mathbb{H}_{\lambda_l}$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce power sums and component characters

nodes.name: Decompose chi_lambda over parts
nodes.statement: Since $Q_{\mathbb{H}}^j \in \mathbb{H}_{\lambda_1} \times \ldots \times \mathbb{H}_{\lambda_k}$, then $$\chi_\lambda(Q_\mathbb{H}^j) = \chi_{\lambda_1 \times \ldots \times \lambda_k}(Q_\mathbb{H}^j) = \sum_{l=1}^k \chi_{\lambda_l} (Q_{\mathbb{H}_{\lambda_l}}^j).$$
nodes.statement_short: Decompose chi_lambda over parts

nodes.name: Decompose sigma_lambda over parts
nodes.statement: Similarly, for $Q_{\mathcal{T}_n}^j = \sum_{i=1}^n M_i^j$, $$\sigma_\lambda (Q_{\mathcal{T}_n}^j) = \sum_{l=1}^k \sigma_{\lambda_l}(Q_{\mathcal{T}_{\lambda_l}}^j).$$
nodes.statement_short: Decompose sigma_lambda over parts

nodes.name: Reduce to length one
nodes.statement: Therefore if we can prove the result of the theorem for every $\mu = (\lambda_l) \in \mathcal{P}^1$, then using the above decomposition of both $\chi_\lambda(Q_\mathbb{H}^j)$ and $\sigma_\lambda (Q_{\mathcal{T}_n}^j)$ we can extend this to $\sigma_{\lambda}$ and $\chi_\lambda$ for every strict $\lambda$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to length one

nodes.name: Induction on n in steps of two
nodes.statement: Fix $m \in \mathbb{N}$. We prove this statement by induction on $n$ with steps of length two. Note that for $n=0$ and $n=1$, all operators act by zero, hence the base cases are trivial.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on n in steps of two; trivial base cases

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: Suppose the result is true for $n-2$, so: $$\sigma_{(n-2)}(P_{\mathcal{T}_{n-2}}^{2m}) = \chi_{(n-2)} (P_{\mathbb{H}}^{2m}).$$ Now, considering that $\sigma_{(n-2)}$ is the restriction of $\sigma_{(n)}$ to $\mathcal{T}_{n-2}$, $$\sigma_{(n)}(P_{\mathcal{T}_{n}}^{2m}) - \sigma_{(n-2)}(P_{\mathcal{T}_{n-2}}^{2m}) = \sigma_{(n)}( (2M_{n-1})^{2m} + (2M_{n})^{2m}).$$ By Corollary \ref{actionT} this is equal to \begin{equation*} \begin{split} \sum_{i=1}^{t} (i-1)^m(i)^m - \sum_{i=1}^{t-2} (i-1)^m(i)^m & = (t-2)^m(t-1)^m + (t-1)^m(t)^m\\ & = (t-1)^m ((t-1 + 1)^m + (t-1 -1 )^m ) \\ &= (t-1)^m (\sum_{l=0}^m {m\choose l} (t-1)^{m-l} (1^l + (-1)^l))\\ & = (t-1)^m\sum_{\substack{l \in {0,\ldots ,m} \\\text{ and even} }} 2 {m\choose l} (t-1)^{m-l}\\ & = \sum_{j = 0}^{\lfloor \frac{m}{2} \rfloor} 2 {m \choose 2j} (t-1)^{2m-2j}. \end{split} \end{equation*} We know that $$\chi_{(t)}(P_{\mathbb{H}_t}^{2m}) - \chi_{(t-2)}P_{\mathbb{H}_{t-2}}^{2m},$$ is just the action of the $x_{t}$ and $x_{t-1}$. Expanding out $P_{\mathbb{H}_t}^{2m}$ and explicitly writing $\chi_{(t)}(P_{\mathbb{H}_t}^{2m})$ using Lemma \ref{actionH}, we know that $$\chi_{(t)}(P_{\mathbb{H}_t}^{2m}) - \chi_{(t-2)}P_{\mathbb{H}_{t-2}}^{2m}= \sum_{j = 0}^{\lfloor \frac{m}{2} \rfloor} 2 {m \choose 2j} (t-1)^{2m-2j}.$$ Therefore we have shown that the inductive step holds.
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step

nodes.name: Difference on the T_n side
nodes.statement: Suppose the result is true for $n-2$, so: $$\sigma_{(n-2)}(P_{\mathcal{T}_{n-2}}^{2m}) = \chi_{(n-2)} (P_{\mathbb{H}}^{2m}).$$ Now, considering that $\sigma_{(n-2)}$ is the restriction of $\sigma_{(n)}$ to $\mathcal{T}_{n-2}$, $$\sigma_{(n)}(P_{\mathcal{T}_{n}}^{2m}) - \sigma_{(n-2)}(P_{\mathcal{T}_{n-2}}^{2m}) = \sigma_{(n)}( (2M_{n-1})^{2m} + (2M_{n})^{2m}).$$
nodes.statement_short: Difference on the T_n side

nodes.name: Binomial computation via Corollary 7.15
nodes.statement: By Corollary \ref{actionT} this is equal to \begin{equation*} \begin{split} \sum_{i=1}^{t} (i-1)^m(i)^m - \sum_{i=1}^{t-2} (i-1)^m(i)^m & = (t-2)^m(t-1)^m + (t-1)^m(t)^m\\ & = (t-1)^m ((t-1 + 1)^m + (t-1 -1 )^m ) \\ &= (t-1)^m (\sum_{l=0}^m {m\choose l} (t-1)^{m-l} (1^l + (-1)^l))\\ & = (t-1)^m\sum_{\substack{l \in {0,\ldots ,m} \\\text{ and even} }} 2 {m\choose l} (t-1)^{m-l}\\ & = \sum_{j = 0}^{\lfloor \frac{m}{2} \rfloor} 2 {m \choose 2j} (t-1)^{2m-2j}. \end{split} \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Binomial computation via Corollary 7.15

nodes.name: Same difference on the H side via Lemma 7.16
nodes.statement: We know that $$\chi_{(t)}(P_{\mathbb{H}_t}^{2m}) - \chi_{(t-2)}P_{\mathbb{H}_{t-2}}^{2m},$$ is just the action of the $x_{t}$ and $x_{t-1}$. Expanding out $P_{\mathbb{H}_t}^{2m}$ and explicitly writing $\chi_{(t)}(P_{\mathbb{H}_t}^{2m})$ using Lemma \ref{actionH}, we know that $$\chi_{(t)}(P_{\mathbb{H}_t}^{2m}) - \chi_{(t-2)}P_{\mathbb{H}_{t-2}}^{2m}= \sum_{j = 0}^{\lfloor \frac{m}{2} \rfloor} 2 {m \choose 2j} (t-1)^{2m-2j}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Same difference on the H side via Lemma 7.16

nodes.name: Inductive step holds
nodes.statement: Therefore we have shown that the inductive step holds.
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step holds

nodes.name: Conclude by induction
nodes.statement: Hence $$\sigma_{(n)}(P_{\mathcal{T}_{n-2}}^{2m}) = \chi_{(n)} (P_{\mathbb{H}}^{2m})$$ by induction.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude by induction
